title: TB4-12715
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellant appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) alleges to be a citizen of Somalia. The Appellant appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.

The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and determine the Appellant to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant asks that the RAD send the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.

The Appellant is relying on new evidence pursuant to Section 110(4); however, the Appellant is not requesting an oral hearing pursuant to Section 110(6)1 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA or Act).2 The Minister is not intervening in the appeal.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed. BACKGROUND/ALLEGATIONS

The Appellant alleged that he is a citizen of Somalia. He belongs to the Ashraf clan, sub-clan Hassan. In 2007, his father was killed by members of the XXXX clan. After the death of his father, the Appellant's mother feared for his safety both from the XXXX clan, and the Al Shabaab militants who forcefully recruited youth to their army. In XXXX 2008, the Appellant's mother was able to arrange for the Appellant to flee Somalia and go to live in Kenya. In Kenya, the Appellant lived with a distant relative, XXXX XXXX XXXX ("XXXX"). The Appellant's mother remained in Somalia. The Appellant lost contact with his mother, and has not heard from her since XXXX 2013. In Kenya, the Appellant had no status. The Appellant went to school in Nairobi with a pseudo name, and using fake documents. In Kenya, the Appellant feared that he would be detected by the authorities to be a Somali, and thus would face deportation to Somalia. XXXX helped the Appellant with his travel out of Kenya; she assisted him financially, and in finding an agent who facilitated the Appellant's travel to Canada. The Appellant fears persecution upon return to Somalia at the hands of large Somali clans and Al Shabaab.

Accompanied by a smuggler, the Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2014. The Appellant entered Canada using a fraudulent German passport. On September, 30, 2014, the Appellant filed his claim for refugee protection at an inland office of the Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC).

The Appellant's claim was heard on November 28, 2014. In the decision of December 8, 2014, the RPD rejected his refugee claim. The RPD found that the Appellant, on a balance of probabilities, has failed to establish his identity with credible and trustworthy evidence.
The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its assessment of his identity. ADMISSIBILITY OF EVIDENCE SUBMITTED ON APPEAL

The Appellant submits that he is relying on new evidence, pursuant to Section 110(4) of the IRPA, an affidavit of his relative in Canada named XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ("affiant XXXX").3 The Appellant submits that this affidavit was not available to him at the rejection of his claim because his relative was hesitant to be involved in his case. The Appellant submits that his relative only agreed to provide this affidavit to him post-hearing.4

As provided for in Section 110(3) of the IRPA, with certain exceptions, the RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD and may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and person subject to the appeal. Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides the RAD with factors to consider in assessing a document's newness and reasonableness of its availability. Section 110(4) of the IRPA indicates that, "the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection." RAD Rule 3(3)(g)(iii) directs applicants to include an explanation of how the documentary evidence submitted to the RAD meets the requirements of Section 110(4) of the IRPA.

In his Affidavit5 and in his Memorandum,6 the Appellant explains why his proposed new evidence should be accepted by the RAD. The RAD reviewed and assessed the Appellant's proposed new evidence, as per Section 110(4) of the IRPA and in the context of the totality of the Appellant's evidence adduced at the RPD, including the recording of the RPD's proceedings.

The RAD notes that the Appellant is eighteen years old. The RAD finds the Appellant provided little reliable and satisfactory probative evidence at the RPD to establish his identity as a citizen of Somalia. Moreover, the evidence in this case shows that the Appellant did not make a reasonable and diligent effort to obtain reliable and satisfactory probative documentation to support his identity as a Somali national. The evidence adduced at the RPD shows that the Appellant was living with the affiant XXXX, the Appellant's relative, at the time of his RPD hearing; the affiant XXXX accompanied the Appellant to the RPD office for the hearing of the claim. The RPD noted in its reasons that the Appellant lived with his distant relative, who waited outside the hearing room. The RAD considered the Appellant's submissions that his relative was hesitant to be involved in his case, and that his relative only agreed to provide the affidavit to him post-hearing. The affiant XXXX, however, is the Appellant's relative; the Appellant was living with him at the time of his RPD hearing. Considering that the Appellant forwarded little reliable and satisfactory probative evidence to the RPD and that the Appellant was represented by competent counsel at the RPD, and in the circumstances of this case, the RAD finds it reasonable for the Appellant to have presented this evidence, the affidavit of affiant XXXX XXXX to the RPD prior to the rejection of his claim. Therefore, the RAD finds the Appellant's proposed new evidence does not satisfy the factors set out in Section 110(4) of the IRPA.
Based on the above, the RAD does not admit the above as new evidence.

In assessing the appeal, the RAD is guided by the recent Huruglica7 decision which outlines the approach that the RAD should take as an appellate body in reviewing the first level decisions of the RPD. Justice Phelan has indicated that the RAD conducts a hybrid appeal and is required to review all aspects of the RPD's decision and comes to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. This authority comes from the broad remedial powers of the RAD, including the power to set aside and substitute the RPD's determination that, in its opinion, should have been made as per Subsection 111(1)(b) of the IRPA. The RAD can recognize and respect the conclusions of the RPD on issues such as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching its conclusion; however, the RAD has equal or greater expertise to the RPD in the interpretation of country conditions evidence. The RAD is not restricted to intervening on facts where there is a palpable and overriding error. It is not necessary for the RAD to find an error on some standard of review basis in order to trigger its remedial power.
The RAD adopts and applies the Huruglica case law in this appeal.

Section 106 of the IRPA states that: The Refugee Protection Division must take into account, with respect to the credibility of a claimant, whether the claimant possesses acceptable documentation establishing identity, and if not, whether they have provided a reasonable explanation for the lack of documentation or have taken reasonable steps to obtain the documentation.

Rule 11 of the RPD Rules states that: The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing their identity and other elements of the claim. A claimant who does not provide acceptable documents must explain why they did not provide the documents and what steps they took to obtain them.

Further, instructions accompanying the Basis of Claim (BoC) state: You must show the IRB evidence of who you are by giving the IRB official documents with your name and date of birth on them. For example, you can give a passport, national identity card, birth certificate, school certificate, driver's licence, military document, professional or religious membership card. If you do not have documents like this with you, you need to do everything you can to get them immediately. If you still cannot get these documents, you will need to explain the reason for this at your hearing and show that you did everything you could to get them. Attach two copies of all documents (identity, travel or other documents) that you have with you now to support your claim for refugee protection, including documents that are not genuine, documents that you got in an irregular or illegal way or by giving information that is not true, and documents you used that do not really belong to you. In addition to the documents listed above, you can include proof of membership in political organizations, medical or psychological reports, police documents, business records, news clippings, visas, and airplane, train or bus tickets.

Referring to the Federal Court case Su,8 the RPD stated, "The onus is on the [Appellant] to produce acceptable documentation establishing his or her identity. This is a high burden, as it should be." The RPD also referred to the Federal Court case Duale,9 in which the Court noted that "It is up to the claimant to establish his identity and he must make genuine, substantive effort to do so."

The RPD wrote that the burden rests on the claimant to establish, with credible and trustworthy evidence, on a balance of probabilities, that he is who he says he is, and that he is a national of Somalia.

Based on the totality of the evidence adduced in this case, the RAD finds the Appellant, on a balance of probabilities, has failed to produce sufficient reliable and trustworthy probative evidence to establish his personal identity and his identity as a national of Somalia as required by Section 106 of the IRPA and Rule 11 of the RPD Rules.

The Appellant has submitted little reliable and satisfactory probative evidence of him ever residing in Somalia, or Kenya. The Appellant's own evidence shows that he went to school on a pseudo name and using fake documents. He had not submitted any of those documents to the RPD. The RAD finds the Appellant provided no documents regarding his alleged domicile in Somalia for twelve years, and thereafter for six years, in Kenya. The evidence shows that an agent was engaged for the Appellant's alleged travel from Kenya to Canada. The Appellant allegedly travelled with a smuggler to Canada using a fraudulent German passport. There are no documents whatsoever showing any of the alleged arrangements that had been made on the Appellant's behalf for his travel from Kenya to Canada. The Appellant has high school education; he is fluent in English, and speaks Somali. Based on the above, the RAD finds it reasonable to expect that the Appellant would have some documentation to corroborate his identity, or at the very least be able to show that he has made a reasonable and diligent effort to obtain any such documentation. The evidence on the record, including the recording of the RPD's proceedings, shows that the Appellant did not make a reasonable and diligent effort to obtain reliable and satisfactory probative documentation to establish his personal identity, and his identity as a citizen of Somalia.

Based on the foregoing analysis and reasons, the RAD concurs with the RPD's finding to give the Appellant's documentation, 1) an affidavit from someone whom the Appellant met in a chance encounter in Kenya and then it happened that the Appellant ran into the same person at a restaurant frequented by Somalis in Toronto and 2) a scratch-notes-style document from the so-called XXXX XXXX XXXX, little weight towards establishing the Appellant's personal or national identity.

The Appellant allegedly lived in Somalia for twelve years, before his mother sent him to live with a relative in Kenya. In addition to a lack of reliable and satisfactory probative documentation to support his personal and national identity, the RPD's adverse credibility findings relating to the Appellant's identity are also based on other concerns including: a. The Appellant's inadequate knowledge about the area and the wider vicinity where the Appellant allegedly lived in Somalia.10 b. The unreliability of the witness testimony at the RPD because the witness provided insufficient details to authenticate the Appellant's identity.11

In a recent case, the Federal Court12 stated the following on the issue of identity: There is no doubt that the onus is on a claimant to establish his or her identity with documentary evidence, and, if such documents are not provided, to explain what steps were taken to obtain them.13 Consequently, a lack of acceptable documents without a reasonable explanation for their absence, or the failure to take reasonable steps to obtain them, is a significant factor in assessing the credibility of a claimant.

In addition to a lack of sufficient reliable and satisfactory probative evidence to support his personal and national identity, the RAD finds the Appellant has failed to show that he had made a reasonable and diligent effort to obtain reliable and satisfactory probative documentation to corroborate his personal and national identity. In these respects, the RAD concurs with the RPD's negative credibility findings.

Based on the foregoing analysis and reasons, the RAD finds the Appellant has failed to establish with credible and trustworthy probative evidence, on a balance of probabilities, that he is who he says he is, and that he is a national of Somalia.

Since the RAD cannot establish the Appellant's personal identity and his country of nationality; the RAD cannot find the Appellant to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of Canada's protection. Justice Blanchard noted in Ipala,14 "The decisions of this Court indicate clearly that a refugee claim must be dismissed once the Board determines that the identity of the claimant has not been proven."15 Justice Blanchard in Ipala,16 citing Justice Beaudry's reasoning in Najam17 stated, "The proof of a claimant's identity is of central importance to his or her claim. ...[I]f the identity of the claimant is not proven, the claim must fail; that means the Board need not pursue an analysis of the evidence in relation to other aspects of the claim...."
Based on the above analysis and reasons, the RAD finds the Appellant's claim fails.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.
